          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Pursuant  to  our  judgment  dated
09.07.2018, the Government of NCTE of Delhi

## Page 157

6
filed the compliance reports. Thereafter, on
21.01.2026,  we  directed  the  Government  of
NCTE of Delhi to take action against the
erring hospitals who have failed to comply
with our order dated 09.07.2018.
2. Thereafter,  fresh  compliance
affidavit(s) was filed by the Government of
NCTE of Delhi enlisting the hospitals who
fall short in complying with this Court's
order dated 09.07.2018.
3. On 24.02.2026, we issued notice to the
hospitals  mentioned  in  paragraph-6  of  our
order as to why proceedings  should not be
taken against them for committing contempt of
Court for violating this Court's order; and
why the concessions granted to them by the
Government shall not be withdrawn.
4. The hospitals, to which notices were
issued  by  this  Court,  submitted  their
compliance  affidavits  upon  which,  we
appointed  Mr.  Sanjay  Jain,  learned  senior
counsel and Mr. Ninad Laud, learned counsel
as  Amicus Curiae  to compile and prepare a
chart  on  the  basis  of  the  compliance
affidavits filed by the hospitals.
5. A report was filed by the learned Amici
on 10.05.2026. In view of the report of the

## Page 158

7
learned Amici, this Court, vide order dated
13.05.2026, requested the learned  Amici, to
convene  a  joint  meeting  of  the  following
stakeholders/ officers;
a. The  amici,  Shri  Sanjay  Jain,
Senior Advocate and Shri Ninad Laud,
Advocate.
 
b.  Dr.  Kusum  Arora,  Superintendent
Nursing  Home  and  EWS  (Economically
Weaker Section) In-charge, GNCTD.
 
c.  Noticee  hospitals  through  their
medical  superintendent/authorised
officers.
d.  Secretary  of  the  Department  of
Health & Family Welfare (MoHFW), GNCTD.
e.  Director,  Land  and  Development
Office, Government of India.
f. Senior Officers from the land owning
agencies. 
g. Deputy Commissioner level officer
from Municipal Corporation of Delhi,
New Delhi Municipal Council and Delhi
Cantonment  Board.  h.  Director  level
officer  from  Delhi  Development
Authority. 
i. Joint Secretary, Ministry of Health,
Central Government.
6. After holding a meeting on 23.05.2026,
as ordered by this Court, the learned Amici
has filed an SOP titled as  “Delhi EWS Free
Treatment Standard Operating Procedure, 2026”.

## Page 159

8
7. Learned  senior  counsel  and  learned
counsel appearing for the noticee hospitals
would submit that the copy of the said SOP has
been supplied to them only a day before i.e.
on 27.07.2026 and therefore, they need time to
peruse the SOP and suggest improvements, if
required, so that after this Court adopts the
SOP, it should be properly implemented.
8. Having  heard  learned  amici;  learned
senior counsels and learned counsel appearing
for the parties, we feel that the SOP should
also dwell on the provisions/ procedures to be
taken for admitting emergency patients as soon
as  any  such  patient  is  brought  to  the
hospital.
9. At  this  stage,  learned  Amici,  would
refer to Clause-7 of the SOP which speaks
about  “verification  at  the  hospitals  and
emergencies”. Clauses 7.2 and 7.3 of the SOP
in particular, deal with the procedure to be
adopted by the hospitals when emergency EWS
patients are brought to the hospitals. Clause-
20 of the SOP which deals with the denial
protocol  and  Clause-20.5  thereof,  provides
that a hospital shall not be permitted to deny
treatment  to  an  EWS  patient  requiring  an

## Page 160

9
emergency treatment only on the ground that
he/ she has exhausted the EWS quota for the
Month.
10. Let  a  revised  SOP  be  filed,
especially dealing with the procedure to be
followed or is followed as to the emergency
treatment  required  by  the  EWS  patients.
Suggestions on this particular aspect, as also
on the SOP already filed by the learned Amici,
by the noticee hospitals shall be submitted
to the learned  Amici  within two weeks from
today.  Thereafter, revised SOP to the above
effect shall be filed by the learned  Amici
within the next one week.
11. Learned  Amici,  would  state  that
Yatharth Hospital, Model Town  (Noticee no.32)
has neither attended the meeting on 23.05.2026
nor responded to the notice issued by this
Court. 12. Let notice be issued to the
Yatharth Hospital, Model Town explaining as to
why proceedings for committing contempt of
Court may not be initiated against it and the
responsible  representative/  medical
superintendent of the said hospital may not be
sent behind bars. The medical superintendent
of the  Yatharth Hospital, Model Town , shall
remain in attendance before the Court on the

## Page 161

10
next date of hearing. Notice to this effect be
served on the Medical Superintendent of the
Yatharth  Hospital,  Model  Town through  the
concerned Station House Officer.
13. Post the matter on 09.09.2026.

1. Heard.
2. These proceedings relate to a transfer petition filed by the wife seeking a
transfer  of  the  proceedings  initiated  by  the  respondent  –  husband  in
Matrimonial Suit No.139/2024.
3. Considering the relationship between the parties, this Court was of the
view  that  parties  can  explore  the  possibility  of  arriving  at  a  settlement.
Accordingly, after lengthy discussions and deliberations, the parties are said to
held talks and have settled the dispute, and in furtherance of the same, an
agreement has  been  entered  into  between  the  parties  on  14.02.2026.  The
terms of settlement as agreed to between the parties are as under:
1

## Page 179

“5. Both the parties hereto have arrived at an amicable settlement on the
following  terms  and  conditions  for  dissolution  of  marriage  by  mutual
consent:-
A.  That the parties have agreed that the Respondent-husband
will pay to the Petitioner-wife a total sum of Rs. 17,00,000/- (Rupees
Seventeen Lakhs Only) towards full and final settlement of all her
claims towards her permanent alimony, Stridhan, maintenance (past,
present, future) and any other claim whatsoever.
B. It is agreed between the parties that they will move an application
jointly  before  the  Hon'ble  Supreme  Court  under  Article  142  of
Constitution  of  India  for  invoking  inherent  powers  of  the  Hon'ble
Supreme Court praying for divorce by mutual consent as parties are
staying separately since 14.03.2021 i.e. for the last more than four
years and there is irretrievable break down of the marriage.
C. It is further agreed between the parties that if Hon'ble Supreme
Court is pleased to allow application filed by both the parties under
Article  142  of  Constitution  of  India  then  both  the  parties  shall
withdraw all the above mentioned cases filed by them against each
other and any other cases that they or their family members have
filed  against  each  other  or  their  family  members.  The
Respondent/husband will pay to the Petitioner/ Wife a total sum of Rs.
17,00,000/- (Rupees Seventeen Lakhs Only) via RTGS/NEFT /Online
Transfer/DD in the account Bearing No. 33140415477, SBI Bank, IFSC
-SBIN0010426, Branch Bandel, Chinsurah, Hooghly, in the account of
Petitioner/wife.
D.  The  Respondent/husband  will  pay  amount  of  Rs.  17,00,000/-
(Rupees Seventeen Lakhs Only) in 5 installments is as under:-
I. The Respondent/Husband has paid the first installment an
amount of Rs. 2,00,000/- (Rupees Two Lakhs only) in favour of
the Petitioner/ wife by way of Online Payment through Yono
App from his SBI Account No. 37778173770 in the Petitioners
above mentioned SBI bank account at the time of signing of
the present Settlement agreement today i.e. 14.02.2026.
II. The Respondent/Husband shall pay Second installment an
amount of Rs. 5,00,000/- (Rupees Five Lakhs only) in favour of
the  Petitioner/  wife  by  way  of  demand  draft/RTGS/  Online
Payment on or before 28th February 2026.
III.  The  Respondent/Husband  shall  pay  third  installment  an
amount of Rs. 4,00,000/- (Rupees Four Lakhs only) in favour of
the  Petitioner/  wife  by  way  of  demand  draft/RTGS/  Online
Payment on or before 31st March 2026.
IV. The Respondent/Husband shall pay Fourth installment an
amount of Rs. 3,00,000/- (Rupees Three Lakhs only) in favour
of the Petitioner/ wife by way of demand draft/RTGS/ Online
Payment on or before 31st May 2026.
V. The Respondent/Husband shall pay Fifth / final installment
an amount  of Rs.  3,00,000/- (Rupees Three  Lakhs only) in
favour of the Petitioner/ wife by way of demand draft/RTGS/
Online Payment on or before 31st July 2026.
2

## Page 180

6. That the Petitioner and the Respondent have agreed that none of them
will initiate any other legal action or complaint against each other or against
the family members of each other in respect of their matrimonial dispute in
future.
7. That subject to the aforesaid terms, the parties have resolved all the
disputes amicably in relation to the marriage and have been left with no
claims against each other or their respective family members.
8. That by signing this Agreement the parties hereto solemnly state and
affirm that they have no further claims or demands against each other
including maintenance, or any movable or immovable property and all the
disputes and differences have been amicably settled by the parties hereto
through the process of mediation.
9. The parties undertake to abide by the terms and conditions set out in the
above mentioned Settlement Agreement, which have been arrived with free
will of the parties without any coercion, duress or collusion and parties
undertake not to raise any dispute whatsoever henceforth.
10. The contents of this settlement - agreement have been explained to all
the parties through their respective counsels and they have understood the
same.”
4. Both parties are present before the Court.
5. This Court, having interacted with them, is satisfied that the parties have
understood the contents of the settlement agreement and they have affixed
their signatures voluntarily without any force, threat, or coercion.
6. The petitioner wife acknowledges the receipt of the amount as indicated
in the settlement agreement and also acknowledges the receipt of Rs.17 Lakhs
in full and final settlement and against all her claims and she specifically states
that  she  has  no  further  claims  either  against  the  respondent  or  his  family
members or anyone else connected with their matrimonial dispute.
7. The learned counsels, in token of having identified the parties, have also
affixed their signatures to the settlement agreement.
8. The parties have agreed that the litigations which are pending before
various courts can be put to an end and the following cases are said to be
pending between parties:
“(i) The Petitioner/wife has filed Divorce Petition Matrimonial Suit no. 76 of
2024 before the District Judge at Hoogli, West Bengal.

9. In the light of the aforesaid facts, we are of the considered view that we
have no impediment to accept the settlement.
4

## Page 182

10. All attempts having been made for reunion of parties having failed, and
both parties being well-educated and being ad idem on the issue of parting their
ways, we are of the considered view that continuation of their marriage would
only be an exercise in futility and as such, in exercise of our power vested under
Article 142 of the Constitution of India, we dissolve the marriage solemnized on
25.02.2020 between the petitioner and the respondent.
11. In view of the settlement arrived at and both parties having agreed for
resolving their disputes, continuation of the proceedings aforesaid would not be
warranted.  They  stand  closed,  quashed  and  disposed  of.  The  jurisdictional
courts shall consign the records accordingly. Transfer Petition stands disposed
of.
12. In view of the settlement agreement entered into between the parties and
there being no further claim by the wife against the respondent – husband, the
order of attachment of his salary stands vacated. 
13. In view of the settlement arrived at between the parties, Transfer Petition
(Criminal) Nos.521/2025 and 514/2025 do not survive for consideration. Hence,
they are also disposed of accordingly. 
14. Registry to draw the decree of divorce in the above terms.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

CIVIL APPEAL NO.                OF 2026
[ @ SPECIAL LEA VE PETITION (C) No.26701 OF 2024 ]

O R D E R
Leave granted. 
Three sons of one Dina Bandhu Bhattacharjee were the plaintiffs who
sought  declaration  of  title,  of  Schedule-A  property  and  possession  of
Schedule-B,  lying  within  Schedule-A;  from  which  the  plaintiffs  were
alleged  to  have  been  dispossessed,  by  the  defendants  in  1997.  The
defendants/legal heirs of the original defendant, are the appellants herein
who  are  aggrieved  with  the  impugned  judgment,  which  reversed  the
dismissal of the suit and declared ownership and directed vacant possession
of Schedule-B property.
2. We have to first notice the various orders passed in the two rounds of
litigation.  The  defendant  filed  written  statement  in  the  suit  specifically
admitting  the  ownership  of  ‘A’ Schedule  property  covered  by  Khatian
Page 1 of 7
CA @ SLP(C) No.26701/2024

## Page 193

No.283 and Dag No.361 having an extent of 4 bigha 1 kathas 11 lechas; in
which is comprised ‘A’ Schedule land. The defence was that the defendant
was a tenant of land measuring 1 katha 19 lechas within ‘A’ Schedule. The
defendant produced Rayati Khatian of the tenanted premises as Ext.Ka and
land holding certificate as Ex.Kha. Rent receipts were also produced through
DW1 as Ex.Ga, Ga(1) and Ga(2).
3. The Trial Court framed three issues:
i) Whether the defendant has a Rayati status?
ii) Whether he is evictable?
iii) Whether the plaintiff is entitled to get any relief and the
valuation in the suit?
4. Except the valuation in the suit which was alleged to be undervalued,
all other issues were found against the plaintiff. It was found, based on the
documents, that the defendant had Rayati status and hence he was not liable
to eviction. The plaintiffs’ prayer for declaration was not raised as an issue,
presumably because there was a clear admission of title by the defendant.
The suit was dismissed finding no relief entitled to the plaintiff. A first
appeal  was  taken,  in  which  Annexure  P4  judgment  was  passed  by  the
Appellate Court. The Trial Court judgment was upheld in toto.
5. In a second appeal, there was a remand with a specific direction,
which has been extracted in the impugned judgment; passed in the second
round at the second appeal stage. The extract indicates that the High Court
Page 2 of 7
CA @ SLP(C) No.26701/2024

## Page 194

was concerned with a discrepancy in the identity of the land as emanating
from the pleadings of the parties. Despite the submission on behalf of the
defendant that there were enough material on record to establish the claim
of the defendant; refusing to examine the facts at the second appeal stage,
the  matter  was  remanded.  The  issue  was  again  considered  by  the  First
Appellate Court and Annexure P5 order was passed. At that stage, the First
Appellate Court went into the question of title of the plaintiff, which was
not even framed as an issue in the suit; as we observed, presumably because
of the admission of the defendant. Despite noticing the documents produced
by the defendant, for reason only of not examining the Settlement Officer,
the  First  Appellate  Court  ruled  against  the  Rayati claim  raised  by  the
defendant, still no relief was granted to the plaintiff since he had not proven
the title and ownership.
6. In the impugned order, the High Court, according to us rightly, found
that there was clear admission by the defendant of the plaintiffs’ title. There
could not have been any issue raised on that, which in any case, as we
pointed out, was not raised before the Trial Court. The First Appellate Court
could not have considered the issue; which was not raised before the Trial
Court. We have to notice that the plaintiff and the defendant had not raised
any objection with respect to the issues framed by the Trial Court and they
are bound by it. The defendant, definitely, cannot dispute the plaintiffs’ title
Page 3 of 7
CA @ SLP(C) No.26701/2024

## Page 195

by reason of his admission in his written statement and his claim was also of
being a tenant in the land from which eviction was sought.
7. The High Court, however, found that on issues No.1 and 2 regarding
the Rayati claim and the liability for eviction, the First Appellate Court had
ruled against the defendant. Hence on the basis of the title, eviction was
ordered directing vacant possession of the land to be handed over to the
plaintiff, which is challenged by the legal heirs of the defendant in this
appeal.
8. The High Court noticed that there was no appeal by the defendant
from the order of the First Appellate Court and hence there could be no
Rayati claim set up. We cannot agree, since though the  Rayati claim was
decided,  the  suit  itself was dismissed,  finding  the  plaintiffs to  have  not
established  their  title.  Hence,  when  the  plaintiffs  filed  an  appeal,  the
defendant could have agitated his cause, while supporting the impugned
judgment.
9. Their contention was elaborately dealt with and rejected finding that
the description of the extent of the land shown in Schedule-B is far less than
the land shown in the Khatian receipts. Schedule-B is that drawn up in the
plaint and if the extent claimed is less than that in the possession of the
tenant;  that  cannot  solely  result  in  the  claim  of  tenancy  being  rejected
outright. We have to also immediately observe that the Khatian receipts, the
Page 4 of 7
CA @ SLP(C) No.26701/2024

## Page 196

land holding certificate and rent receipts were brushed aside by the First
Appellate Court at the second stage; finding inevitable the examination of
the Settlement Officer. 
10. In this context, we have to notice the findings of the Trial Court,
which clearly recorded that the Rayati receipts, land holding certificate and
the rent receipts, specifically referred to by us above, were produced by the
defendant  without  any  objection  from  the  plaintiffs,  hence  requiring  no
further  proof.  The  finding  of  the  First  Appellate  Court,  hence,  that  the
Settlement Officer had to be necessarily examined was perverse. The High
Court also failed to notice that, even in the remand order, there was nothing
stated as to the Rayati claim of the defendant. Even if we deem the remand
order to be an open remand, the finding of the First Appellate Court, was
quite in contrast to the finding of the Trial Court, which also ignored the
documents produced, not objected to by the plaintiff.
11. We cannot but hold that the plaintiffs’ title has been established, as
pointed  out  by  the  High  Court,  at  least  in personam, by  virtue  of  the
admission of the defendant. The defendant also established his Rayati claim
and hence is not liable for eviction.
12. The suit, hence, has to be dismissed. We reverse the order of the
learned Single Judge in Second Appeal and restore the order of the Trial
Court dismissing the suit.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.             OF 2026
(@ SLP(C) No.            OF 2026)

RAVI KANT GUPTA        ... APPELLANT
VERSUS
STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH & ORS.       ... RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Leave granted. 
3. These appeals arise from the judgment and order dated 06.10.2023
in Writ-C No. 8139 of 2023 and the order dated 29.01.2024 in Civil
Misc.  Review  Application  No.  128  of  2023,  passed  by  the  High
Court1. In order to appreciate the grievance of the appellant relevant
facts need mention which are stated infra. 
4. The appellant is the owner of residential house bearing No. 8/331,
Vikas Nagar, Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh (premises). The respondent
no. 4 is the son of the appellant whereas respondent no. 5 is the
wife of the appellant. The mother of the appellant is aged about 81
years. She was forced to leave the premises and was forced to reside
1  High Court of Judicature at Allahabad at Lucknow Bench
1

## Page 200

at an old age facility. On 05.06.2022, the appellant preferred an
application before the District Magistrate under the Maintenance
and  Welfare of  Parents  and  Senior  Citizens  Act, 2007 (the  Act)
seeking eviction of respondent no. 4 (son). 
5. The Sub-Divisional Magistrate (SDM) by an order dated 15.11.2022
inter alia held that the premises is the self-acquired property of the
appellant and the son did not permit the mother of the appellant,
namely,  his  grandmother  to  stay  in  the  premises  and  created
nuisance. The SDM directed eviction of the son from the premises. 
6. The son and the wife preferred an appeal under Section 16 of the
Act before the District Magistrate. The District Magistrate by an
order dated 09.08.2023, affirmed the order passed by the SDM and
ordered the son and the wife to handover the possession of the
premises  to  the  appellant.  The  son  and  the  wife,  thereafter,
approached the High Court by way of filing a writ petition namely,
Writ-C No. 8139 of 2023. The High Court on 06.10.2023 noted that
learned Single Judge 2 has held that the Act did not empower the
authorities to pass an order of eviction. Accordingly, the High Court
quashed the orders dated 15.11.2022 and 09.08.2023 and allowed
the writ petition.
7. Being aggrieved, the appellant filed a review application which was
2  Abhishek Tiwari and Another v. State of U.P., 2022 SCC OnLine All 367
2

## Page 201

dismissed on 29.01.2024 by the High Court reiterating the lack of
power  in  authorities  of  ordering  eviction  under  the  Act.  In  the
aforesaid factual background this appeal has been filed.
8. We  have  heard  the  learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  and  the
respondent nos. 1 to 3 as well as the respondent no. 4 and have
perused the records. 
9. The measure of a civilized society is often reflected in the dignity,
respect  and  security  it  affords  to  its  elderly.  Across  cultures,
religions, and civilizations, senior citizens have been regarded not
merely as dependents requiring care, but as repositories of wisdom,
experience, and collective memory whose guidance enriches families
and society alike. Article 21 of the Constitution as interpreted by
this Court and Article 41 of the Constitution envisage a social order
that protects the vulnerable and enables every individual to live
with dignity throughout the course of life. This commitment finds
statutory expression in the Act, enacted to ensure that advancing
age  does  not  become  synonymous  with  neglect,  insecurity,  or
indignity.  In  light  of  the  aforesaid  constitutional  mandate,  the
Parliament  has  enacted  the  Act.  The  provisions  of  the  Act
incorporate the values deeply rooted in our country’s civilizational
ethos which revere the mother and the father as divine. The Act is
3

## Page 202

intended to provide a speedy remedy for the senior citizen. 
10. Under Section 7 of the Act, the tribunals have been constituted
which have power under Section 8 of the Act to conduct an inquiry
following  a  summary  procedure  with  powers  of  a  Civil  Court.
Section 27 of the Act explicitly bars the jurisdiction of the Civil
Courts.  It  is  a  well-settled  legal  proposition  that  where  an  Act
confers a jurisdiction, it impliedly also grants the power of doing all
such acts, or employing such means, as are essentially necessary to
its execution 3. On this analogy, we have no hesitation in holding
that the tribunal under the Act has power to order eviction in order
to ensure the maintenance or protection of a senior citizen.  
11. It is noteworthy  that a three-Judge Bench of this Court 4, while
dealing with claims arising out of the provisions of the Act and the
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 held that
the tribunal under the Act may have the authority  to order an
eviction if it is necessary and expedient to ensure the maintenance
and protection of a senior citizen or a parent. It was further held
that  eviction  would  be  an  incident  of  enforcement  of  right  to
maintenance  and  protection.  Taking  into  account  the  aforesaid
observations, a two-Judge Bench of this Court 5, held that tribunal
3  Income Tax Officer Cannanore v. M.K. Mohammed Kunhi, 1968 SCC OnLine SC 71
4  S. Vanitha v. Deputy Commissioner, Bengaluru Urban District & Ors., (2021) 15 SCC 730
5  Samtola Devi v. State of U.P. & Ors., 2025 SCC OnLine SC 669
4

## Page 203

under the Act may order eviction if it is necessary and expedient to
ensure the protection of senior citizens.  Another two-Judge Bench
of this Court6 reiterated the same view. 
12. We are in respectful agreement with the view taken by this Court on
multiple occasions. The reliance placed by the High Court on its
decision7 is misconceived. 
13. For  the  foregoing  reasons,  the  impugned  judgment  dated
06.10.2023 passed in Writ-C No. 8139 of 2023 and the order dated
29.01.2024 passed in Civil Misc. Review Application No. 128 of
2023 are set aside and the orders passed by the authorities under
the Act ordering eviction are restored. 
14. In the result, the appeals are allowed. There shall be no order as to
costs.

2. The  High  Court  of  Punjab  &  Haryana  at
Chandigarh,  by  a  judgment  and  order  dated  09th
April,  2026,  has  dismissed  the  application  of  the
appellant for  bail  in  anticipation  of  arrest. This
appeal is directed against such judgment and order.
3. Appellant figures as an accused in FIR No.0074
of 2025 dated 24 th April, 2025 registered at Police
Station  Sadar  Ratia,  District  Fatehabad,  Haryana
under Sections 3(5) & 318(4) of the Bharatiya Nyaya
Crl. Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No.9940/2026 1

## Page 207

Sanhita, 2023 1 with Sections 336(3), 338, 340(1),
340(2), 61(2) and 238, BNS added, later on. 
4. We have heard learned counsel appearing for
the parties.
5. It appears from the counter-affidavit that the
appellant  has  joined  investigation  by  presenting
himself before the investigating officer on 01 st June,
2026, in  terms  of  an  earlier  order  of  this  Court.
Pursuant to a disclosure statement of the appellant,
his mobile phone has also been recovered and taken
possession by the investigating officer.
6. Charge-sheet  has  been  filed.  Prosecution
proposes  to  record  the  evidence  of  11  (eleven)
witnesses  to  drive  home  the  charges  against the
appellant, but none has been examined till date.
7.  T rial is, therefore, likely to take some time to
conclude.
8. Having regard to the nature of allegations and
taking an overall view of the matter, we are of the
considered  opinion  that  the  appellant’s  custodial
1 BNS
Crl. Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No.9940/2026 2

## Page 208

interrogation is not necessary and that he may be
admitted to an order for grant of bail in anticipation
of arrest.
9. Accordingly,  we  set  aside  the  impugned
judgment and order.
10. It is directed that in the event of the appellant
being arrested, he shall be released on bail on terms
and conditions to be imposed by the trial court.
11. If  the  appellant’s  presence  is  required  for
further interrogation, the investigating officer will be
at  liberty  to  call  upon  the  appellant  to  appear
whereupon he shall do so by attending the police
station  failing which liberty is granted to bring any
such omission to the notice of the trial court and
seek cancellation of bail.
12. Needless  to  observe,  the  appellant shall not,
directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat
or  promise,  dissuade  any  person  acquainted  with
the facts of the case from disclosing such facts to
any police officer or to the court.

13. We clarify that the observations made in this

aforesaid terms.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).       OF 2026
[@ SLP (C) NO.5843 OF 2026]
 RAJINDER INFRASTRUCTURE PVT. LTD.                 …Appellant(s)
VERSUS
 MINISTRY OF DEFENCE & ORS.                              …Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The instant Civil Appeal arises out of the interim order dated 3 rd
December 2025 passed by the High Court of Sikkim at Gangtok in Writ
Petition (Civil) No. 75 of 2025 (“Impugned Order”). 
3. Short facts relevant for disposal of this appeal are that on 5 th May
2025, the Border Roads Organisation (“BRO”), a specialised statutory
agency under the Ministry of Defence, Government of India, invited bids
for  the  construction  of  the  Rishi-Rongli-Kupup  road  in  Sikkim,  an
infrastructure  project  of  strategic  importance  to  our  nation.  The
Appellant (Rajinder Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.) as well as the Respondent
No. 6 (Hill Brow Metallics & Construction Pvt. Ltd.) participated in the
1

## Page 225

tender process. Pursuant to that process, the Appellant furnished an
undertaking on 18th June 2025 and submitted an ‘Integrity Pact Format’.
On the basis of these and other documents, the Appellant was declared
as qualified with respect to the Technical Bid on 4 th October 2025. The
Financial Bid was opened on 22 nd October 2025 and given that the
Appellant was found to be the lowest bidder, it was declared as L-1.
Consequently, even Letter of Acceptance (LOA) was also issued on 17th
November 2025. The Respondent No. 6 was declared as L-2.
4. On 6th November 2025, the Respondent No. 6 issued legal notices
to the Appellant and BRO alleging that the Appellant had not disclosed
the incomplete ongoing projects and past debarment orders passed
against it by the Greater Mohali Area Development Authority (GMADA)
and the Punjab Urban Development Authority (PUDA), public authorities
established  by  the  State  of  Punjab,  with  respect  to  participation  in
tenders. Proceeding further, on 12th November 2025, Respondent No. 6
filed a Writ Petition before the High Court challenging the results of the
Technical  Bid.  The  Respondent  No.  6  prayed  that  the  Summary  of
Technical Evaluation be set aside, that BRO be injuncted from issuing a
Letter  of  Award  (“LOA”)  in  favour  of  the  Appellant,  and  that  the
Respondent No. 6 be declared as the selected bidder with respect to
both the Technical and Financial Bids. Pending disposal of the Writ
Petition, the Respondent No. 6 prayed that the Summary of Technical
2

## Page 226

Evaluation and all consequential tender processes be stayed.
5. By  the  order  impugned  before  us,  the  High  Court  stayed  the
Summary of Technical Evaluation dated 4 th October 2025 along with
consequential steps with respect to the LOA dated 17th November 2025.
The  Appellant,  being  the  successful  bidder,  is  before  this  Court,
challenging the legality and validity of the interim order passed by the
High Court. 
6. The Appellant contends that when the Writ Petition came up for
hearing before the High Court for the first time on 28 th November 2025,
its counsel entered appearance and sought a copy of the Writ Petition.
The  High  Court  listed  the  matter  on  the  next  working  day,  i.e.,  1st
December  2025,  and  reserved  the  case  for  interim  orders.  The
Appellant’s grievance is that sufficient opportunity was not accorded to it
to contest the Writ Petition. The Appellant further contends that certain
important facts related to the case could not be placed before the Court
as the High Court proceeded to pronounce the interim order. It is also
submitted  that  the  project  is  of  national  importance  and  is  to  be
undertaken in extreme weather conditions. 
7. Mr. Anil Kaushik, the Learned Additional Solicitor General, supported
the Appellant and argued that projects like this cannot be delayed and
that the High Court could not have passed such an interim order unless
there are compelling circumstances, which according to him did not
3

## Page 227

exist at all.
8. Having considered the matter in detail, we are of the opinion that the
reasoning  adopted  by  the  High  Court  with  respect  to  the  interim
direction virtually disposes of the Writ Petition on merits. This could not
have been the approach for passing interim orders in matters relating to
evaluation of bids, particularly for projects of strategic importance to this
nation. Without expressing any further opinion on the merits of the case
as the order impugned is interim in nature, we are of the opinion that
interest of justice will be subserved if we set aside the interim directions
and request the High Court to take up the Writ Petition and dispose it of
on merits as expeditiously as possible.
9. For the reasons stated above, the appeal stands allowed, the interim
order passed in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 75 of 2025 dated 3 rd December
2025 is set aside. The High Court will now take up and dispose of the
Writ Petition expeditiously.

deliberations, the parties have settled their dispute, and in furtherance of the
same, an agreement has been entered into between the parties on 12.05.2026.
The terms as agreed to between the parties are as under:

Delay condoned. Leave granted. 
2. The appeal is against the concurrent finding of conviction by 
three Courts. The learned Counsel for the appellant, at the outset, 
submitted t hat the matter has been settled with the de-facto 
complainant. The de-facto complainant is also said to be present 
online. However, the fact remains that two of the accused are not 
before us; one, to whom the land was sold and the other, who was 
a witness  to the sale deed . We hence proceeded to hear the 
matter on merits, since a settlement recorded by us , could 
interfere with civil rights. 

## Page 243

Page 2 of 4 
3. The de-facto complainant is said to have filed a complaint 
against 11 accused. A1 is the mother; who is now no more and A2, 
A4, A7 and A8 are A1’s children . A3 is the son of A2 , and A5 and 
A6 are sons of A4 . A9 to A11 are acquaintances. The allegation 
was that a land having an extent of two acres sold by A1 to the de-
facto complainant was later sold by A1 -A8, to A9.  A10 and A11 
were witnesses to that document. The sale deed was alleged to be 
a forged document. We are surprised that cognizance was taken 
on the allegations levelled, leave alone the finding of guilt, which 
was confirmed by the Appellate Court and even the High Court. 
4. The facts disclosed are that A1 along with her husband sold 
two acres of property to one Thulasiammal, the de-facto 
complainant, in the year 1977. The vendee’s daughter, Dev aki 
was in possession of the land and on her death, she was survived 
by her husband and five children. The land was partitioned 
amongst the five children equally and a very small portion, 1¾ 
cents was sold to a third party. Later, A1 to A8 sold the land to A9 
by a sale deed of 03.10.2008. Numerous witnesses were paraded 
to show the encumbrance recorded, the possession and so on and 
so forth. The Trial Court found A1 to A11 guilty of offences under 
Sections 120B, 465 , 468, 471 , 420 read with Section 34 of Indian 

## Page 244

Page 3 of 4 
Penal Code, 18601 and sentenced them to various periods with fine 
imposed and default sentences. 
5. We are unable to find the ingredients of any of the 
provisions afore-mentioned, on the allegations levelled. The land 
itself is said to be in the possession of the heirs of the deceased 
daughter of the de-facto complainant. Hence there cannot even be 
levelled an allegation of dishonest delivery of property. Though 
A9 is said to have purchased the property , she was not even 
impleaded before us and she is not a party to the settlement. The 
other accused who is absent before us, is A11, who is said to have 
witnessed the sale deed. The witnesses to the document, A10 and 
A11 and A9 who purchased the property cannot at all be accused 
of any complicity, if at all , there is a crime coming out from the 
facts. The entire foundation of the finding of guilt seems to be a 
forensic examination carried out , of the finger print in both the 
documents, which admittedly is of A1. The 1977 document was 
executed by A1 alone and the later document was executed by 
A1 to A8. A2 to A8 submits that they were unaware of the earlier 
sale. As far as A1 is concerned, she is no more, as of now. 
 
1 For brevity, ‘the IPC’ 

## Page 245

Page 4 of 4 
6. As we observed , we cannot take note of a settlement, 
arrived at between the parties, which is inconsequential, insofar 
as a criminal case is concerned , that too where cognizable 
offences are charged , which cannot be compounded. However, 
on the allegations raised and the evidence led, we do not find the 
ingredients of the offence having been made out. 
7. Hence, we set aside the impugned order of the High Court 
as also the order of the Trial Court and the Appellate Court. The 
appellants/accused are acquitted of the offence and set at liberty. 
8. Insofar as the accused A9 and A11 who are not parties to the 
appeal, though in their absence, we acquit them also, since we 
have found on facts that there can be absolutely no culpability on 
the accused.  
9. The appeal stands allowed. 
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

appellant in R.C.C. No. 2607/2018 for the offences punishable

4. Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  submitted  that  the

## Page 249

2
appellant is the second wife of the former husband of the
respondent No. 1 and the allegation against her is that she had
submitted a forged decree of divorce with her first husband in
order to show that she was competent to marry the former husband
of the respondent No. 1.
5. It was submitted that such contention was based solely on
the judgment and decree of divorce granted to the appellant from
her former husband, in which the date of the marriage of the
appellant to her former husband had been wrongly typed. It was
submitted that the complaint was that later on, the wrong date
was corrected by cutting the incorrect date by the clerk
concerned. However, when a complaint was filed, there was a
full-fledged inquiry made by the Court concerned and ultimately,
it has been held that there was no forgery and the correction
was made bona fide as it was an error apparent on the face of
the record. It was further submitted that once the decree and
grant of divorce to the appellant from her previous husband is
not in dispute, there cannot be any culpability, much less
criminal culpability, attributed to her. 
6. Learned counsel submitted that the date of marriage of the
appellant to her first husband pales into the background when
the fact remains that such marriage was dissolved prior to
marriage of the appellant with the former husband of the

## Page 250

3
respondent No.1. It was further submitted that the appellant had
filed only the certified copy of the decree of divorce as she
had received from the Court which was prior to the error being
noticed and corrected by the concerned Court clerk. 
7. Learned counsel for the State of Maharashtra submitted that
in the inquiry, it has been found that there was no role or
deliberate act or collusion of the Presiding Officer and nobody
had suffered because of such correction/alleged criminal act. 
8. Respondent  No.1  vehemently  opposed  the  prayer  of  the
appellant and submitted that the appellant had produced a
document which had incorrect recording and the correction made
without going through the legal way, would amount to the
document being forged in the eyes of law. It was submitted that
the appellant also did not file the corrected version. 
9. Having considered the matter in its entirety, we find that
a case for interference has been made out. The appellant cannot
be faulted for producing before a Court, a decree, certified
copy of which was obtained by her. It is not in dispute that a
decree of divorce was granted to the appellant from her former
husband prior to the date of her contracting marriage with the
former husband of the respondent No.1. It is also not in dispute
that the said decree was later on corrected in the original
records and the so-called correction was also with regard to the

## Page 251

4
date of marriage of the appellant with her former husband, which
probably  would  not  be  very  relevant  in  the  facts  and
circumstances of the case. 
10. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The order impugned
stands  quashed.  The  appellant  is  discharged  from
R.C.C.No.2607/2018.

Heard  Mr.  Brijender  Chahar,  learned  Additional  Solicitor
General for the appellant and Mr. Sukesh Ghosh, learned counsel for

2. Leave granted.
3. The present appeals arise out of a claim case filed by the
respondent seeking compensation for the death of his father, who
died in a rail accident upon falling from a running train in the
year 2001. The respondent filed Claim Application No.A/699/2002
seeking compensation of Rs.4,00,000/- (Rupees Four Lakhs) which was
dismissed by the Railway Claims Tribunal, Kolkata vide order dated
06.10.2010. The petitioner herein assailed the said order in appeal
bearing FMA No.531/2012 before the High Court of Calcutta wherein
the  impugned  order  was  passed  granting  compensation  of
Rs.8,00,000/- (Rupees Eight Lakhs) along with interest of 6% per
annum from the date of filing of claim application.

## Page 260

2
4. Though, we have been assisted by learned counsels on merits
but ultimately, the issue has narrowed down as to what would be the
quantum of compensation payable to the respondent.
5. According to the learned Additional Solicitor General for the
appellant, at the relevant point of time when the accident occurred
on 17.06.2001, there was a policy to pay Rs.4,00,000/- (Rupees Four
Lakhs) compensation to the dependent(s)/claimant(s), which was
revised in the year 2017 and enhanced to Rs.8,00,000/- (Rupees
Eight Lakhs).
6. In terms of our earlier order dated 06.01.2026, Rs.8,00,000/-
(Rupees Eight Lakhs) has been paid by the appellant to the
respondent.
7. Learned counsel for the respondent submits that the amount of
compensation may be enhanced as per the order dated 04.11.2025
passed by this Court in C.A. No.13872 of 2025 (Shrikumar Gupta &
Anr. v. Union of India), where in a case of rail accident, this
Court has granted interest @9 per cent from the date of the award.
8. Having considered the matter in its entirety and taking into
account the fact that even as per the case of the appellant,
Rs.4,00,000/- (Rupees Four Lakhs) had to be paid to the respondent
soon after the accident in the year 2001 itself, which was not paid
and  only  upon  order  dated  06.01.2026  passed  in  the  present
proceeding, Rs.8,00,000/- (Rupees Eight Lakhs) had been paid, we
deem it appropriate to award interest @9 per cent on Rs.4,00,000/-
(Rupees Four Lakhs) from the date of the accident till realisation.
The same be computed and the difference be paid to the respondent
within four weeks from today.

1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant, who has been arraigned as an accused in FIR No.200 of 2025
for the offence punishable under Sections 20(b)(ii)C, 24 of  Narcotic Drugs
and  Psychotropic  Substances  Act,  1985  (NDPS  Act),  Section  14A  of
Foreigners Act, 1946 and Section 3(3) of the Passport (Entry to India) Act,
1920, is seeking for being enlarged on regular bail.
4. It is the  case  of the  prosecution that, acting on a tip-off, the  police
intercepted a White Hyundai Car on 15.07.2025 bearing Registration No.TN-
50-BX-0006 and found the appellant and co-accused were traveling in the
said car and on search of the vehicle being conducted, in the presence of
the T ehsildar, they found 12 packets containing 26 kgs of ganja in the boot
of the car and as such appellant and co-accused were arrested. It is also the
1                                                                                        SLP(CRL.) NO.9006 OF 2026

## Page 265

case of the prosecution that the total recovery linked to the larger syndicate
is 306 kgs.
5. Several contentions have been raised in support of grant of bail. Suffice
to state for prima facie satisfaction for grant of bail in the instant case can
be satisfied from the arrest memo which records the date and time of arrest
of  appellant  as  15.07.2025  at  23.15  hours.  It  also  reflects  that the  FIR
No.200 of 2025 had already been registered whereas the FIR which is at
Annexure  P1  would  reflect  that  it  was  registered  at  00.26  hours  on
16.07.2025. It might be true that there is a gap of about an hour. However,
this  is  an  intriguing  question  which  requires  to  be  explained  by  the
prosecution during the course of trial. Any discussion if entered into by this
Court, is likely to prejudice rights of either of the parties. Hence, we leave at
it.
6. In the light of the aforestated facts and the contention of the appellant
that he had already been arrested on 14.07.2025 and to substantiate the
said defence, an application had been moved by the appellant before trial
court for preservation of CCTV footage of three police stations, and said
application came to be allowed by the trial court by order dated 25.11.2025
and the status report filed thereof would indicate that the two police stations
and the office of the Superintendent of Police from whom a CCTV footage
was sought for, was not available purportedly on the ground of sudden hype
in the power supply at these three places. Without commenting anything on
the said issue and leaving it open to the trial court Judge to examine the
same on its own merits, after considering the experts opinion, if any, we
deem  it  proper  to  enlarge  the  appellant  on  regular  bail,  however,  with
stringent conditions in order to allay the apprehension of the prosecution.
2                                                                                        SLP(CRL.) NO.9006 OF 2026

## Page 266

7. Accordingly, appeal is allowed. Impugned order is set aside. Appellant is
ordered to be released on regular bail on such terms and conditions as the
jurisdictional Court may deem fit to impose and also on the condition that
appellant would appear three times a week, every Monday, Thursday and
Saturday between 11:00 am to 2:00 pm before the jurisdictional police and
mark his attendance till the conclusion of the trial apart from directing him
to  appear  on  all  dates  of  hearing  before  the  trial  court  except  when
exempted for any specific reason.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant, who has been visited with an FIR 199 of 2021 registered
for the offences under Sections 302, 364, 452, 148 and 149 of Indian
Penal Code, 1860 (IPC), is seeking for being enlarged on regular bail.
4. The gist of the prosecution case is that the deceased couple were
abducted and murdered by group of persons on account of couple
getting married without the consent of the members of the family.
Though initially the appellant was not indicted in the FIR, subsequently
on the basis of the statement of co-accused persons, appellant came to
be  roped  in  as  an  accused  and  the  role  attributed  as  per  the
chargesheet  is  that  he  was  a  member  of  unlawful  assembly  who
forcefully trespassed into the house of the complainant, abducted the
deceased  couple  and  subsequently  murdered  them.  In  fact,  the
prosecution has heavily relied upon the CCTV footage/CDR location to
1                                                                                 SLP(CRL.) NO.8266 OF 2026

## Page 270

form the basis of implication. The said CCTV footage which was played
before the trial court reflected that it was corrupt and non-functional
and accordingly finding has been recorded by the learned trial Judge
vide order dated 18.05.2023.
5. In the light of the aforestated facts when the case of the prosecution
is viewed, it has to be necessarily noted at this stage ( prima facie) that
the appellant was not implicated as an accused in the FIR though it was
registered against 16 persons and taking note of the fact that appellant
has undergone more than 4 years 5 months and the trial is progressing
at a snail’s pace and the trial is being adjourned at the instance of the
prosecution, we are of the considered view that continued incarceration
of the appellant would not be warranted at this stage.
6. Accordingly,  appeal  is  allowed.  Impugned  order  is  set  aside.
Appellant is ordered to be released on regular bail on such terms and
conditions as the jurisdictional court may deem fit to impose and also
on the condition that appellant would appear before the jurisdictional
trial  court  on  all  dates  of  hearing  except  when  exempted  for  any
specific reason.

State or the complainant would be at liberty to move the jurisdictional
trial court seeking cancellation of bail granted by this Court by filing an
appropriate application. In the event of such an application being filed,
the  trial  court  shall  consider  the  same  on  its  own  merits  and  in
accordance with law.

1. This appeal is directed against the order passed
by the Division Bench of the Gauhati High Court
dismissing the appellant's appeal against the order
passed by the learned Single Judge which in turn had
allowed the respondents' writ petition directing the
Deputy Commissioner to entrust the case to the learned
Senior most Assistant Deputy Commissioner (ADC) of the
Station who shall deal with the matter without being
influenced by the Deputy Commissioner concerned who
had passed the order dated 17.01.2013.
2. The appellant challenged the directions issued by
the learned Single Judge by preferring intra-court
appeal which was dismissed by observing that the
matter is required to be independently examined by the
statutory authority and only thereafter, the appellant
can be allowed to take further steps.
1

## Page 275

3. The issue pertains to use of respondents' land
for erection of high power transmission line known as
"400 kV Silchar-Bongaigaon D/C transmission line".
Admittedly, one tower of the said project was to be
erected over the respondent's land on which the high
tension  line  would  be  installed.  The  respondents
objected to erection of the tower and the line on the
ground that the same is being done without acquiring
the land and without paying any compensation.
4. During the pendency of this civil appeal, learned
counsel for the appellant made a statement before this
Court that the work of laying of high tension line on
the subject area was re-aligned and now the high
tension line is not passing through the land belonging
to the respondents. On this statement being made, this
Court directed the appellant to file an affidavit to
which the respondent shall file counter affidavit.
5. Complying with the above direction, the appellant
filed its affidavit to which reply affidavit was filed
on behalf of Respondent Nos.1(i)-(vii). It was stated
in  the  reply  affidavit  that  the  appellant  had
determined the compensation by assessing the value of
trees @ Rs.6,48,252/- and Rs.4,97,484/-  and despite
drawing the cheque for the sum of Rs.5,82,336 and
2

## Page 276

Rs.4,46,239/-, the appellant had withheld the payment
of compensation for the trees taking advantage of the
interim order passed by this Court.
6. Copies of the above stated cheques along with the
calculation have been annexed to the reply affidavit.
In the rejoinder affidavit filed by the appellant, the
statements  made  by  the  respondent  in  the  reply
affidavit has not been traversed. Thus, the said
statements  has  remained  un-controverted  and  it
deserves to be accepted.
7. It appears on the date the learned single Judge
and division Bench of the High Curt has decided the
matter, the compensation was yet to be determined,
however, now the calculation has been done and the
cheque has been prepared.
8. Therefore, in the above view of the matter, we
dispose of this civil appeal directing the appellant
to make payment of the amount for which the cheque has
already  been  drawn  to  the  respondent  along  with
interest @6% per annum. The amount already paid to the
respondent at any point of time during the assessment
of  compensation  for  the  period  for  which  the
respondent's land were used shall be adjusted. The
payment shall be made within three months from today
3

## Page 277

subject to the respondents submitting the proof of
ownership of the land.
9. The Civil Appeal stands disposed of.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.     OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) No.12554/2026)
ASWIN ..... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF TAMIL NADU ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1.   Leave granted.
2.   We have heard Mr. R. Basant, learned senior counsel for
the  appellant  and  Mr.  B.  Karunakaran,  learned  counsel
representing the State of Tamil Nadu.
3.  By filing this appeal, appellant has assailed the
legality and correctness of the Order dated 05.08.2025,
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Madras (briefly
the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), in Criminal OP No.19100/2025
rejecting the prayer for bail of the appellant.
4.  Appellant  is  an  accused  (accused  No.4)  in  Crime
No.110/2025,  registered  at  Race  Course  Police  Station,
Coimbatore, under Sections 8(c), 22(b), and 29(1) of the
Narcotic  Drugs  and  Psychotropic  Substances  Act,  1985,
1

## Page 285

(Briefly the ‘NDPS Act’ hereinafter).
5.   Appellant is in custody since 03.03.2025.
6.  This Court had issued notice on 13.07.2026. However,
State has not filed counter affidavit. Since this is a
matter pertaining to bail and personal liberty, we are not
inclined to grant further time to the respondent-State.
7.  Allegation against the appellant is that acting on a
secret information, the police apprehended a person near VCV
Shishu  Vidyodaya  School,  Coimbatore  and  recovered  a
polythene bag from him. Upon opening the bag, it was found
to contain contraband meant for supplying to school and
college  going  children.  Later  on,  after  chemical
examination, the contraband was found to be methamphetamine.
Following disclosure statement made by him, appellant and
others came to be arrested. It is stated that from the
appellant, approximately, 53 grams of methamphetamine came
to be recovered.
8.   Learned Senior Counsel has drawn the attention of the
Court to the seizure memo (Annexure P-3) and submits that
the aforesaid seizure was made from 3 accused persons i.e.,
the appellant along with Abdul Saleem and Azarudeen. Abdul
Saleem is accused No.5 and Azarudeen is accused No.6. It is
not mentioned as to how much quantity of the contraband was
recovered from each of the aforesaid 3 accused. He further
submits that investigation is complete whereafter charge
sheet has been submitted on 26.05.2025. He also submits that
the other 2 accused persons; Abdul Saleem and Azarudeen have
2

## Page 286

been granted bail by the High Court. Therefore, further
continuance  of  detention  of  the  appellant  may  not  be
warranted.
9.   Learned State counsel submits that since recovery was
made from the person of the appellant, Section 37 of the
NDPS  Act  would  be  applicable.  The  extent  of  quantity
recovered from each of the aforesaid 3 accused can only be
determined during the course of the trial.
10.  Submissions made by learned counsel for the parties
have received the due consideration of the Court.
11.  As already noted above, the appellant is in custody
since  03.03.2025.  Investigation  is  complete  whereafter
charge sheet was submitted before the Special Court on
26.05.2025. On a query by the Court, learned senior counsel
for the appellant submits that charges have not yet been
framed, though, more than one year has gone by since
submission of the charge sheet. That apart, prosecution has
cited 12 witnesses.
12.  In the circumstances, we are of the view that appellant
may be enlarged on bail. For that purpose, let the appellant
be produced before the concerned Special Court within a
maximum period of 7 days from today, whereafter he shall be
enlarged on bail on such terms and conditions as may be
deemed appropriate.
13.  Consequently, impugned order of the High Court dated
05.08.2025 is set aside.
14.   Criminal Appeal is accordingly allowed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

GUNINDRA SARMA @ GUNIN SARMA & ANR. APPELLANTS
                        
   VERSUS
HARMOHAN PATHAK & ORS.                 RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. This appeal is directed against the order dated 05.12.2025, whereby the
High Court affirmed the order dated 08.02.2024 and 26.07.2024, whereunder
the  trial  Judge  had refused the  prayer  for  adjournment  sought  for  by  the
defendant, and had also rejected the prayer of the newly impleaded defendant,
namely, the appellants herein, to adduce evidence.
4. Having heard the learned counsels appearing for the parties, and on
perusal of the impugned order as well as the order of the trial Court, we find
that  there  is  some  justifiable  ground  on  the  part  of  the  learned  counsel
appearing for the respondents’ contending that the appellant No.1 herein has
only been formally impleaded as defendant No.1 and he was already on record
as defendant No.6 and by mere change of nomenclature, it would not change
the status and as such, Ms. Atiga Singh,  learned counsel appearing for the
1

## Page 304

respondents would be correct in contending that the impugned order would not
warrant interference.
5. Having  said  so,  we  notice  Order  X  Rule  (2)  sub-rule  (5),  it  clearly
mandates that proceedings against any person added as defendant would be
deemed to have begun only on the service of summons as an impleaded party.
In the instant case, as rightly agreed by both the parties, that appellant No.1
was already there on record as defendant No.6 namely in the capacity of being
a member. On account of his status from that of a member to that of an office
bearer having got changed, he has been impleaded as first defendant. Thus, the
impleaded  applicant  would  have  a  right  to  further  prosecute  the  case
independently. In order to avoid any technical plea being taken by the present
appellants in future and to put a quietus to such plea being raised, we deem it
proper to permit appellants to lead the evidence, if any.
6. However, to allay the apprehension of the respondents/plaintiffs that on
this ground the appellants are likely to protract the proceedings, it would suffice
to direct the appellants to tender their evidence on the next date of hearing
without fail and if they fail to do so, the opportunity provided to them by this
order  would  automatically  get extinguished.  It is  made  clear that both the
parties shall cooperate with the trial Court in expeditiously disposing of the suit
and, at any rate, within an outer limit of four months from today. 
7. This Court while issuing notice had directed the appellants to deposit
costs to cover the costs of respondent No.1 for appearing before this Court or in
other words who have been perforced to appear before this Court. Accordingly,
the appellants have deposited ₹50,000 in this Court. The amount in deposit in
this Court is ordered to be transmitted by the Registry of this Court to the
2

## Page 305

jurisdictional  trial  Court  for  being  disbursed  in  favor  of  respondent  No.1  –
plaintiff on proper identification.
8. With the aforesaid observations, the appeal stands disposed of by setting
aside the impugned order and modifying the order of the trial Court to the
extent noted hereinabove.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

1. Petitioner claims to be a juvenile as on 15.06.2015
i.e., the date of commission of the offence. In respect of
the  juvenility  claim  set  up  by  the  petitioner,  on
18.11.2025,  after  considering  the  submissions  made  on
behalf of the petitioner, we had passed the following
order:
“1. The petitioner has set up a juvenility
claim based on school leaving certificate
dated 30.08.2016 issued by Saint Vianney
High School, Lachhadagarh, which discloses
petitioner’s date of birth as 25.06.1998.
Further, an additional affidavit has been
filed  annexing  a  school  transfer
certificate  issued  by  Primary  School,
Kulaanda, District Simdega, Jharkhand. The
second certificate is dated 03.05.2008 and
it  discloses  that  the  petitioner  got
admitted in the school on 04.04.2005 and
left the school on 03.05.2008. His entry in
the school was in Class-III.
2.  From  above,  it  is  clear  that  both
certificates annexed by the petitioner are
not regarding the school first attended by
the petitioner. In such circumstances, we
deem  it  appropriate  to  require  the
petitioner to submit a certificate of the
school where he first attended. The learned
counsel for the petitioner prays for and is
allowed four weeks time to file such an
affidavit.
3. List this matter in the third week of
January, 2026.”
2

## Page 325

2. Pursuant to the above order, an affidavit has been
filed on behalf of the petitioner stating therein that the
petitioner had informal early childhood education and no
official records are available.  Even the date of birth
certificate of the petitioner issued by any authority
which maintains the record of births and deaths is not on
record.  
3. In such circumstances and having regard to the fact
that the plea of juvenility was not raised either before
the Trial Court or before the High Court, and even in the

raised, we do not find a justifiable reason to direct an
inquiry on the claim of juvenility. Consequently, the
application of the petitioner claiming juvenility on the

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Permission  to  file  Special  Leave  petition  is
granted in Diary No.42432/2026.
2. These two petitions are tagged with each other and
have been heard together. In Special Leave Petition
(Crl.) No.10344/2026, the petitioner(s) have questioned
the registration of FIR No.259/2025 on the ground that
it would be a second FIR in respect of the allegations
covered by an earlier FIR, namely, FIR No.8/2025.
3. The other petition emanates from an order of the
High Court dated 19.06.2026 whereby investigation of FIR
No.8/2025 and FIR No.259/2025 has been clubbed and
entrusted to a Special Investigation Team headed by an
IPS Officer to be constituted under orders of the
Director General of Police, (HoPF, Chennai).
4. In the first petition, we had not accepted the
contention that FIR No.259/2025 was second FIR and,
2

## Page 329

therefore, notices were issued limited to the prayer for
transfer of investigation.
5. Having regard to the fact that investigation of FIR
No.08/2025 and FIR No.259/2025 has been clubbed and
assigned to a special investigation team, the question
that now arises for our consideration is limited to the
validity of the order of the High Court dated 19.6.2026.
6. The learned counsel for the petitioner in Special
Leave Petition Diary No.42432/2026 submits that since
the  first  FIR,  namely,  FIR  No.8/2025,  relates  to
Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Department, it would be
appropriate that investigation is carried out by the
said  Department  and  not  assigned  to  a  Special
Investigation team.
7. We have perused the order passed by the High Court.
Paragraphs 18 and 19 of the impugned order would reveal
that there are serious allegations about the cash,
allegedly recovered, being planted. The High Court also
has referred to some CCTV footage, which was viewed by
the High Court, showing a person, carrying a package,
entering  the  office  the  previous  night.   In  such
circumstances, the High Court, though did not express
any  opinion  on  the  aforesaid  aspect,  deemed  it
appropriate to constitute a special investigating team
to investigate both FIRs.
8. As it is well settled that no accused has a right
to choose its investigation agency, having regard to the
3

## Page 330

facts noticed in the order passed by the High Court, we
are of the view that once a special investigation team
has  been  constituted  and  both  cases  appear  to  be
interlinked, it is appropriate that the investigation is
carried out by a common agency, and since that common
agency appointed by the High Court comprises of high
ranking officers, we decline to entertain these special
leave petitions.
9. Both these petitions are, accordingly, dismissed.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner-Corporation is aggrieved with the impugned
judgment of the High Court, more specifically with respect to
1

## Page 336

SLP(C) No.23152/2026
the  cost  imposed  of  Rs.1  lakh.  The  1 st respondent  had
challenged the award of a contract to the 3rd respondent herein
by the petitioner-Corporation despite the 1 st respondent being
L-1. The 1st respondent’s bid was 9.9% below the estimated cost
while that of the 3rd respondent’s was 9.22% below. Despite the
1st respondent being the lowest bidder, he was excluded, was
the  allegation.  This  resulted  in  prejudice  to  the  1 st
respondent, direct financial loss to the public exchequer and
unjust enrichment to the 3 rd respondent, was the contention
before the High Court. 
2. The impugned order found unsatisfactory the explanation for
the rejection of 1 st respondent’s bid and though in public
interest, the award of the contract was not interfered with,
the 1st respondent was granted Rs.1 lakh as costs. 
3. We heard Mr. Anil Kaushik, learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the petitioner and Ms. Ankita Sharma, learned counsel
appearing for the respondent-State. However, none appeared for
the first respondent despite service of notice. 
4. Mr. Anil Kaushik, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
petitioner-Corporation submitted that the 1 st respondent’s bid
was  found  non-responsive  since  he  failed  to  submit  a
clarification, despite a communication having been issued. The
communication issued by the Corporation was in the email
2

## Page 337

SLP(C) No.23152/2026
address disclosed in the bid documents. The 1 st respondent
contended that they did not receive the communication and
there was another email address used for submitting the tender
documents. The High Court erroneously found the procedure
adopted to be wrong, holding that the email address in which
the communication was sent was neither disclosed by the
petitioner for the purpose of submitting the bid documents nor
used at any stage of the tender process. 
5. We find from the arguments recorded that the learned counsel
appearing for respondent No.2 specifically argued that the 1 st
respondent was directed to furnish clarification regarding
non-submission of mandatory details in Annexure A2. A further
communication was issued informing the 1 st respondent that in
the absence of a response, the bid would be found technically
non-responsive and ineligible. The email id used by the
Corporation  was  the  one  provided  in  the  bid  documents,
strictly in terms of Clause 6 under the Note in the tender
conditions.  
6. We see from Annexure 1, the tender documents, that Clause 6
specifically provided thus: -
“6. Bidder must submit their phone no. and Email-id
along with details address of correspondence.” 
7. We, hence, find no error having been occasioned by the
3

## Page 338

SLP(C) No.23152/2026
Corporation and it was the High Court which failed to notice
that the email id, in which the Corporation issued two
communications with respect to the clarification and the
thrust of cancellation; if no response was made, in the
address furnished by the 1st respondent in the bid documents.
 
8. We hence set aside the impugned judgment of the High Court,
specifically deleting the cost imposed on the 1st respondent. 
9. The Special Leave Petition stands disposed of with the above
directions. 
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal arises from an order of the High Court of
Judicature  for  Rajasthan,  Bench  at  Jaipur  dated
25.03.2026  whereby  the  regular  bail  prayer  of  the
appellant in connection with First  Information  Report
(FIR) No.485 of 2024 registered at P.S. Barauni, District
Tonk was rejected.
4. The submission on behalf of the appellant is that there
is a serious issue as to whether the victim is a minor;
besides, the victim in her deposition during trial has
not  supported  the  prosecution  case.   In  such
circumstances, it is submitted, the appellant, who has
suffered incarceration for a period of about 14 months,
is entitled to be released on bail, pending trial.
5. The learned counsel for the State has opposed the prayer
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.8875/2026
1

## Page 344

for bail on the ground that though victim may have been
declared hostile, the Forensic report indicates presence
of semen stain on the undergarment of the victim. 
6. Having regard to the fact that the victim has been
declared hostile, and there is also an issue in respect
of the real age of the victim, without expressing any
opinion on the merits of the prosecution case, we are of
the view that the appellant is entitled to be released on
bail, at this stage.
7. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed. The order passed by
the High Court rejecting the bail prayer of the appellant
is set aside.
8. The appellant shall be released on bail on such terms
and conditions as the trial court may deem fit to impose
in the facts and circumstances of the case.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand    disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CIVIL APPEAL NOs. 11103-11104 OF 2017
ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES        Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
CHARUL MANU                                    Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. These appeals arise out of the Judgment and Order
dated  14.03.2016  passed  by  the  National  Consumer
Disputes  Redressal  Commission  [in  short,  “the
Tribunal”] in First Appeal Nos. 469 of 2008 and 508 of
2008, by which the Tribunal has dismissed the appeal
filed by the appellant – AIIMS and allowed the appeal
filed by the complainant (respondent herein).   
2. It is an admitted position that pending disposal
of the appeals, the entire amount deposited by the
appellant has been withdrawn by the respondent.
3. The  Tribunal,  by  the  impugned  order  dated
14.03.2016, has recorded the following findings :-
“We have no hesitation in arriving at
the  conclusion  that  referring  the
Patient, who was in a grave condition,
to  Safdarjung  Hospital,  was  sheer
negligence on the part of the treating
doctors, and the time spent in his
shifting  undoubtedly  proved  to  be
fatal. Furthermore and admittedly even
the  facility  of  adequately  equipped
ambulance was not provided for shifting

## Page 348

2
of the Patient. It is pertinent to note
that in the written version, except for
highlighting the objectives with which
AIIMS  was  established,  a  specific
averment  in  the  Complaint,  to  the
effect  that  the  attending  doctors
refused to provide a "Mobile Ambulance
Coronary  Care"  has  not  been
controverted. No reason is forthcoming
as to why this life saving facility was
not made available and the Patient,
admittedly under AMI, was tossed from
one  hospital  to  another  like  a
chattel.”
4. Having heard learned counsel appearing for the
appellant  as  well  as  the  respondent-in-person  at
length, we are of the opinion that the circumstances
in which the patient came to the hospital as also the
situation, in which the hospital did not have a bed to
treat  the  patient,  coupled  with  giving  necessary
succor  and  referring  the  patient  to  Safdarjung
Hospital, the treatment at Safdarjung Hospital on
30.07.1997, and then the subsequent return to AIIMS,
gives us an impression that there is no negligence on
the part of AIIMS.
5. However, in view of the fact that the patient and
his attendant had traumatic times shifting from AIIMS
to Safdarjung and then back to AIIMS, though there is
no deficiency/negligence on the part of AIIMS, we are

## Page 349

3
of the opinion that interest of justice will be
subserved  by  not  interfering  with  the  amount  of
compensation granted to the respondent. As the said
amount has already been withdrawn, we see no reason to
interfere with the judgment and order passed by the
National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission to
this extent. 
6. The appeals are disposed of in terms of the above
order.
7. Pending  interlocutory  application(s),  if  any,
is/are disposed of.

O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard  learned  counsel  for  the
parties.
3. This  appeal  arises  from  an  order
dated 16.04.2026 passed by the High Court of
Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh rejecting
the regular bail prayer of the appellant in
connection with FIR No. 171/2025, registered
at P.S. ANTF, Sector 79, SAS Nagar. 
4. The submission of the learned counsel
for the appellant is that admittedly there
1

## Page 356

is  no  incriminating  recovery  from  the
appellant and the allegations against the
appellant are to the effect that he was in
contact with the main accused. It has been
submitted  that  the  appellant  has  been
falsely  implicated.  Earlier  also,  the
appellant was implicated in a case involving
small quantity in which he has been admitted
to bail. 
5. The  learned  Counsel  for  the  State-
respondent has opposed the prayer for bail
but could not dispute that there is no
incriminating recovery from the appellant in
connection with the present case.
 
6. Having  regard  to  the  submissions
noticed  above,  without  expressing  any
opinion on the merits of the case, we are of
the view that the appellant is entitled to
be released on bail pending trial. 
7. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed.
2

## Page 357

The order passed by the High Court rejecting
the regular bail prayer of the appellant is
set aside.
8. The appellant shall be released on
bail on such terms and conditions as the
trial court may deem fit to impose in the
facts and circumstances of the case.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.

O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard  learned  counsel  for  the
parties.
3. This  appeal  arises  from  an  order
dated 01.04.2026 passed by the High Court of
Madhya  Pradesh  at  Gwalior  rejecting  the
regular bail prayer of the appellant in
connection  with  Crime  No.  242/2025,
registered  at  P.S.  Kotwali,  District
Shivpuri (M.P.).
4. The submission of the learned counsel
for the appellant is that he was an employee
appointed  on  contract  to  outsource  work
relating to data entries. The allegation is
1

## Page 360

that certain money was wrongly transferred
to  the  account  of  the  appellant  and,
thereafter, was siphoned off. It has been
submitted that the appellant has suffered
incarceration for a period exceeding one
year three months and there is no likelihood
of trial being concluded in near future as
several co-accused, who are beneficiaries of
the crime, are absconding. It has also been
submitted that appellant has no previous
criminal  antecedents  and  is  physically
handicapped to the extent of 80 per cent of
which certificate has been enclosed.
5. The  learned  Counsel  for  the  State-
respondent has opposed the prayer for bail
by submitting that it is a case where large
sums of money have been defalcated. Besides,
other accused are absconding and even the
appellant could be apprehended only after a
reward was offered for giving information
about them.
6. Be that as it may, having regard to
the fact that the appellant has suffered
2

## Page 361

incarceration  exceeding  one  year  three
months  pending  trial  and  there  is  no
likelihood of trial being concluded in near
future  as  several  co-accused  have  been
absconding, taking into account that the
appellant has physical disability and has no
previous criminal antecedents, we are of the
view that the appellant is entitled to be
released on bail at this stage.
7. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed.
The order passed by the High Court rejecting
the regular bail prayer of the appellant is
set aside.
8. The appellant shall be released on
bail on such terms and conditions as the
trial court may deem fit to impose in the
facts and circumstances of the case.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.

vide impugned order dated 16.07.2025, refused to interfere and

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. This petition arises from the order passed by the High
Court of Madhya Pradesh dated 24.03.2025 by which the Civil
1

## Page 430

Revision Application preferred by the respondents before us
(original defendants) came to be allowed and, thereby, the
plaint of the suit instituted by the petitioner-Trust
before us came to be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 of
the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 on the ground that the suit
is not maintainable in view of the specific bar of Section
32 of the M.P. Public Trusts Act, 1951 (for short, “the
Act, 1951”).
2. It appears that Section 36(1)(a) of the Act, 1951 was
pressed into service by the plaintiff-Trust.
3. Section 36 of the Act, 1951 provides for an exemption.
Section 36 reads thus:-
“Section 36. Exemption.- (1) Nothing contained in this
Act shall apply to-
(a) A public Trust administered by an agency acting
under  the  control  of  the  State  or  by  any  local
authority.”
4. However, the finding of fact recorded by the High
Court is that the registration of the Trust was not valid
and, therefore, Section 36 would not save the situation.
5. The learned counsel would submit that now the Trust
has obtained a valid registration.
6. If that be so, it shall be open for the petitioner-
Trust to proceed further by availing any appropriate legal
remedy available to it in law on the basis of the fresh
registration.
7. With the aforesaid, the Special Leave Petition stands
disposed of.
2

8. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  also  stand
disposed of.
